lessons.title: Certainty, strength and guideline labels
lessons.objective: Read a guideline's labels: the four GRADE certainty levels and what raises or lowers them, the difference between strength of recommendation and certainty, good practice points and other non-GRADE scales, and why a surrogate outcome is not enough.
lessons.closing: High, moderate, low or very low certainty, per outcome; trials start high and observational studies low. Strength and certainty are judged separately: “strong with ⊕” exists, as an exception that needs justifying. GPP and Level III are expert opinion. A semen parameter is not a live birth.

lessons.title: Reasoning with diagnostic tests
lessons.objective: Calculate and interpret sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and likelihood ratios, always start from the pre-test probability, and recognise when a test, including a commercial panel, cannot inform a decision.
lessons.closing: Sensitivity and specificity belong to the test; PPV and NPV depend on prevalence. Post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR. Without a reference standard or an effect on important outcomes, the result cannot guide a decision.

lessons.title: Absolute risk, NNT and shared decision-making
lessons.objective: Translate relative effects into absolute effects and NNT, communicate risk as NICE recommends, and lead a shared decision, applying it to a typical integrative claim from clinic.
lessons.closing: Always ask “from what to what”. NNT = 1 / absolute difference, rounded up and with its time frame. Natural frequencies, the same denominator, both framings, and doing nothing on the table as an option.

items.title: GRADE certainty: four levels and where each design starts
items.core: GRADE rates the certainty (or quality) of evidence for each outcome at four levels: high, moderate, low and very low. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14]] High means great confidence that the true effect lies close to the estimate; very low means the true effect is likely to be substantially different from the estimate. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]]
items.body:
It is rated per outcome and across the body of studies, not study by study: within the same trials, mortality may stay at high certainty while quality of life ends up lower. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] Randomised trials without important limitations start as high certainty and observational studies without special strengths or limitations as low; case series usually drop to very low. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] Expert opinion is not a level of evidence: it is an interpretation of evidence, and the type of studies behind it should be stated. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]]

With the ROBINS-I tool, non-randomised studies may start as high certainty (and be rated down by up to three levels if a concern is extremely serious), but Cochrane notes that sound non-randomised studies are still usually graded low. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14]]
items.recall: What are the four GRADE certainty levels, and at what level do a randomised trial and an observational study start?
items.pearl: “There are studies” tells you nothing: ask what certainty the outcome your patient cares about has.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: GRADE Handbook 2013, table 5.1 and sections 5 and 5.1.1. Cochrane Handbook v6.5 (2024), ch. 14, key points and section 14.2. Symbols suggested by GRADE: high ⨁⨁⨁⨁, moderate ⨁⨁⨁◯, low ⨁⨁◯◯, very low ⨁◯◯◯ (table 6.4).

items.title: What lowers and what raises certainty
items.core: Five factors can lower certainty by one or two levels: risk of bias, inconsistency of results, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] Three can raise it: a large magnitude of effect, a dose-response gradient, and all plausible confounding having reduced the observed effect. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14]]
items.body: It is not a mechanical sum: GRADE is not a quantitative system, each factor is a continuum that requires judgement, and its merit is that the judgement is explicit and transparent. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] If there are minor concerns about several factors, authors may rate down one level for one or two of them and explain it in a footnote. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] The factors for rating up apply mainly to non-randomised studies: with large effects and no obvious bias, they can reach moderate or even high certainty. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14]]
items.recall: Name the five reasons to rate certainty down and the three to rate it up.

rows.text: Randomised trials without important limitations: start at high certainty
Observational studies: start at low certainty
Rate down 1 or 2 levels: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias
Rate up: large effect (1 or 2 levels), dose-response (1), confounding that would reduce the effect (1)
Result for each outcome: high, moderate, low or very low

visual.alt: GRADE scheme: trials start at high certainty and observational studies at low; five factors lower it and three raise it, giving a final level per outcome.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: GRADE Handbook 2013, tables 5.2 and 5.3 and section 5.1. Cochrane Handbook v6.5 (2024), ch. 14, section 14.2 (figure 14.2.a).

items.title: Strength of recommendation is not certainty of evidence
items.core: The strength of a recommendation reflects the panel's confidence that desirable effects outweigh undesirable ones (or vice versa), and GRADE judges it separately from certainty: there can be weak recommendations with high-certainty evidence and, exceptionally, strong ones with low or very low certainty: GRADE discourages the latter except in five paradigmatic situations (for example, possible benefit in a life-threatening situation or possible catastrophic harm). [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] A real example: ESHRE 2023 recommends ultrasound, preferably 3D, to exclude uterine anomalies in unexplained infertility as a strong recommendation with level ⊕. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
Besides certainty, strength depends on the balance of benefits and harms, on values and preferences (and how much they vary) and on resource use. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] Weak recommendations are also called conditional: most people would want the option but many would not, and each patient needs help to decide in line with her values; a strong recommendation means most people should receive it. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] ESHRE uses the same reading of “strong” and “conditional”, and automatically grades evidence as very low (+OOO) when there are no studies specific to unexplained infertility; so when you see “strong with ⊕”, read the justification to find out what the strength rests on. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

Not even a strong recommendation based on high-quality evidence is a dictate: GRADE warns that it should not be applied by rote to every patient. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]]
items.recall: Can a recommendation be strong with very low certainty? Give an ESHRE example.
items.pearl: Always read both labels: “strong” describes the panel's decision; the ⊕ symbols describe the studies.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: GRADE Handbook 2013, sections 1.2, 6.1, 6.1.1 and 6.1.2 and tables 6.1 and 6.2; section 6.3.2 and table 6.3 (five paradigmatic situations for a strong recommendation with low or very low certainty). ESHRE unexplained infertility 2023: rec. 10 in the list of recommendations (p. 8) and methods annex (p. 109), where evidence without specific studies is graded “very low (+OOO)”.

items.title: Labels that are not GRADE: GPP, NAMS levels and add-on phrases
items.core: In ESHRE guidelines, GPP (good practice point) marks a recommendation based mainly on expert opinion. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] NAMS 2022 grades with levels: I, good and consistent scientific evidence; II, limited or inconsistent evidence; III, mainly consensus and expert opinion. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.body:
The 2023 ESHRE add-ons guideline uses four fixed phrases: “recommended” (applicable to most patients), “can be considered” (after a thorough discussion of benefits and risks and with close monitoring), “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” (may change with more evidence) and “not recommended” (for safety, lack of efficacy or lack of biological rationale; research settings only). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] Of its 42 recommendations, none could be based on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence; the rest rely on low-quality trials, observational data, professional experience or consensus (the guideline's abstract puts this at 95%, although 38 of 42 is 90%). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

GRADE warns that the use of letters and numbers varies widely between organisations and can confuse, so read each guideline's legend before comparing them. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]]
items.recall: What do GPP in ESHRE, Level III in NAMS and “can be considered” in the add-ons guideline mean?
items.pearl: A NAMS Level III or an ESHRE GPP is declared expert opinion: useful, but do not read it as if it were trial evidence.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE unexplained infertility 2023, footnote to the list of recommendations (p. 8). NAMS 2022, grading categories (p. 2). ESHRE add-ons 2023, table 1 (p. 3) and abstract (p. 1). GRADE Handbook 2013, section 6.3.2 and table 6.4.

items.title: Surrogate outcomes: a semen analysis is not a live birth
items.core: GRADE says surrogate outcomes should be used only when data on important outcomes are lacking, and using them usually lowers certainty by one or two levels for indirectness (two when the surrogate is far removed in the causal pathway). [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] The ESHRE add-ons guideline notes that many antioxidant studies used semen parameters or the DNA fragmentation index as surrogate success parameters rather than the pregnancy rate. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.body: In the 2022 Cochrane review of antioxidants for male subfertility, the primary outcome was live birth, but of the 67 studies in the meta-analysis only 12 reported it. [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]] With those 12 trials, antioxidants may increase live births (OR 1.43; 95% CI 1.07 to 1.91; very low certainty), but when studies at high risk of bias were removed there was no longer evidence of an increase (Peto OR 1.22; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.75; 8 trials). [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]] ESHRE concludes that antioxidant therapy is not recommended in assisted reproduction treatment. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.recall: Why is a study showing lower sperm DNA fragmentation not enough to recommend a supplement?
items.pearl: When you hear “improves semen quality” or “lowers fragmentation”, ask: and live births?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: GRADE Handbook 2013, sections 3.4 and 5.2.3. ESHRE add-ons 2023, antioxidants (pp. 27–28) and summary table (p. 31). Cochrane de Ligny et al. 2022, abstract: live birth OR 1.43 with very low certainty, and sensitivity analysis without the high risk-of-bias studies.

items.stem: A meta-analysis of well-conducted observational studies, with no large effect and no dose-response gradient, evaluates a supplement. Under the classic GRADE scheme (without the ROBINS-I tool), at what certainty does this evidence start?

options.text: High, because it is a meta-analysis
options.why: Pooling studies does not change the starting point: GRADE starts from the design of the included studies.

options.text: Moderate
options.why: Moderate is a possible result after rating up or down, not the starting point of an observational study.

options.text: Low
options.why: Correct: observational studies without special strengths or important limitations provide low-certainty evidence.

options.text: Very low, always
options.why: Very low applies, for example, to case series or to evidence rated down for limitations; it is not the starting point of a well-conducted observational study.

items.explanation: Trials without important limitations start as high certainty and observational studies as low. From there, certainty can fall for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision or publication bias, and rise for a large effect, dose-response or confounding that would reduce the effect.

items.stem: In the 2023 ESHRE unexplained infertility guideline, ultrasound (preferably 3D) to exclude uterine anomalies is labelled “Strong ⊕”. How should this be read?

options.text: High-quality trials support it
options.why: A single ⊕ means very low certainty; “strong” refers to the panel's decision, not to the quality of the studies.

options.text: The panel is confident that benefits outweigh downsides for most patients, even though the certainty of evidence is very low
options.why: Correct: GRADE judges strength and certainty separately and, as an exception, allows strong recommendations with low or very low certainty.

options.text: It is a contradiction: with ⊕ only conditional recommendations are possible
options.why: It is not: separating strength from certainty is precisely GRADE's defining feature.

options.text: It is a good practice point (GPP)
options.why: In ESHRE guidelines, GPP is a different label, for recommendations based mainly on expert opinion, and carries no ⊕.

items.explanation: Strength depends on the balance of benefits and harms, on values and preferences and on resources, not only on certainty. That is why the same ESHRE list of recommendations contains “Strong ⊕”, “Strong ⊕⊕⊕” and “Conditional ⊕”. Even so, GRADE discourages strong recommendations with low or very low certainty except in specific situations: when you see “Strong ⊕”, read the justification.

items.stem: In the 2023 ESHRE add-ons guideline, what does the phrase “can be considered” imply?

options.text: It can be applied to most patients and adopted as policy
options.why: That is the definition of “recommended”.

options.text: It can be applied after a thorough discussion of benefits and risks, with close monitoring, follow-up and evaluation
options.why: Correct: this is the definition in table 1 of the guideline.

options.text: It should not be used routinely for now, although this may change with more evidence
options.why: That is the definition of “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”.

options.text: It should only be applied in research
options.why: That corresponds to “not recommended”, for safety, lack of efficacy or lack of biological rationale.

items.explanation: The add-ons guideline does not use GRADE strength but four fixed phrases. Moreover, of its 42 recommendations none rests on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence: the rest rely on low-quality trials, observational data, professional experience or consensus (38 of 42, 90%; the guideline's abstract says 95%).

items.stem: In the 2022 Cochrane review of antioxidants in subfertile men, live births may increase (OR 1.43; 95% CI 1.07 to 1.91; 12 trials; very low certainty). Without the studies at high risk of bias, the result is Peto OR 1.22 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.75). Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: Antioxidants clearly increase live births
options.why: Certainty is very low, and the increase is no longer seen when only the lower risk-of-bias studies remain.

options.text: The benefit is not robust: it depends on studies at high risk of bias, and ESHRE does not recommend antioxidants in assisted reproduction
options.why: Correct: the sensitivity analysis shows no increase, and the authors describe the evidence as inconclusive.

options.text: It proves that antioxidants have no effect at all
options.why: The authors conclude that the evidence is inconclusive, not that the effect is zero.

options.text: Semen improvement should guide the decision, as it is more reliable
options.why: Semen parameters are a surrogate outcome; the one that matters to the couple is live birth.

items.explanation: When an effect disappears after removing the studies at highest risk of bias, the overall result is probably inflated. Add the surrogate outcomes of many studies and the ESHRE recommendation: not recommended in assisted reproduction.

items.title: Sensitivity and specificity: properties of the test
items.core: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease (by the reference standard) who test positive; specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]] In a teaching example of D-dimer against perfusion scanning, 7 of 10 people with embolism test positive (sensitivity 70%) and 77 of 90 without embolism test negative (specificity 85.6%). [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]]
items.body:
A highly sensitive test is hardly ever negative in someone with the disease, so a negative result almost rules it out (SnNOut); a highly specific test is hardly ever positive in someone without it, so a positive result almost rules it in (SpPIn). [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]] Their clinical limitation is that they start from knowing who is ill; in clinic you need the opposite, the probability of disease given a result. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]]

All of this requires a reference standard: STARD 2015 asks for it to be described in detail, its choice justified, and the index test cross-tabulated against it. [[ref:bossuyt-2015-stard]]
items.recall: Define sensitivity and specificity and explain SnNOut and SpPIn.
items.pearl: Without a reference standard there is no sensitivity or specificity to calculate.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Ranganathan and Aggarwal 2018, part 1 (hypothetical teaching example). STARD 2015, items 10b, 11 and 23.

items.title: Predictive values: they depend on whom you test
items.core: PPV is the probability of having the disease with a positive test and NPV the probability of not having it with a negative test; unlike sensitivity and specificity, they depend heavily on the prevalence in the tested population. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]] With the same test (sensitivity 70%, specificity 85.6%), PPV is 7/150 = 4.7% at 1% prevalence, 70/200 = 35.0% at 10% and 210/311 = 67.5% at 30%. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]]
items.body: So even a test with good sensitivity and specificity has a low PPV when the pre-test probability is low, and the authors advise applying tests to people with a high pre-test probability based on symptoms and signs. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]] This often happens when a test becomes cheaper and starts being used indiscriminately in people with a low likelihood of disease. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1]]
items.recall: What happens to a test's PPV when you use it in a low-prevalence population?
items.pearl: At 1% prevalence, only 7 of every 150 positives had the disease.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Ranganathan and Aggarwal 2018, part 1, tables 3a–3c (figures in the text). NPV is 99.6%, 96.2% and 86.9% at prevalences of 1%, 10% and 30%. Hypothetical example.

items.title: Likelihood ratios: from pre-test to post-test probability
items.core: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity) and LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity; they do not change with prevalence (in the D-dimer example, LR+ 4.85 and LR− 0.35 at prevalences of 1%, 10% and 30%). [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2]] To use them: post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR, with odds = probability / (1 − probability) and probability = odds / (1 + odds). [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2]]
items.body:
An LR of 1.0 adds nothing; the further it moves from 1, the more it discriminates, and LRs > 10 or < 0.1 are very useful to establish or exclude a diagnosis. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2]] The same positive D-dimer leaves a probability of embolism of about 67% when the pre-test probability was 30%, and 5% when it was 1%; recalculated (0.43 × 4.85 ≈ 2.08 odds; the article gives 2.04), it is 67.5%, the same value as the PPV at that prevalence. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2]]

Limitations: an LR is only as reliable as the studies it comes from, the pre-test probability must be individualised, and there is no consensus on how to combine the LRs of several tests. [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2]]
items.recall: Write the formulas for LR+ and LR− and how to go from pre-test to post-test probability.
items.pearl: Before ordering a test, estimate the pre-test probability: without it the result cannot be interpreted.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Ranganathan and Aggarwal 2018, part 2 (hypothetical example): LR+ = (7/10)/(13/90) = 4.85; LR− = (3/10)/(77/90) = 0.35. Worked numerical exercise in question 7.

items.title: Accuracy is not usefulness: does the result change anything for the patient?
items.core: GRADE is blunt: if a test fails to improve patient-important outcomes there is no reason to use it, whatever its accuracy; the best design to evaluate it is a trial that randomises diagnostic strategies and measures mortality, morbidity, symptoms, quality of life and resource use. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] When only accuracy studies exist, accuracy acts as a surrogate outcome, and you must ask what will happen to those the test labels as diseased and as healthy under the best available management. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]]
items.body: Accuracy studies are also at risk of bias: if not all tested patients are analysed, or if only healthy controls are included, the accuracy estimates may not reflect performance in practice. [[ref:bossuyt-2015-stard]] That is why STARD 2015 asks, among its 30 items, for the intended use and clinical role of the test, how participants were identified and whether they were a consecutive, random or convenience series, the positivity cut-offs and whether they were pre-specified, and the estimates with their precision (for example, 95% CIs). [[ref:bossuyt-2015-stard]]
items.recall: Why might an accurate test still not be indicated?
items.pearl: For every test, ask before ordering it: what will I do differently with each possible result?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: GRADE Handbook 2013, ch. 7 (diagnostic tests, figure 1 and sections 7.3 and 7.4). STARD 2015, items 3, 7, 9, 12a, 24, 26 and 27.

items.title: Commercial panels without demonstrated validity
items.core: The 2025 international consensus on microbiome testing considers the evidence insufficient to widely recommend routine use in clinical practice (90% agreement) and discourages patients from requesting tests without a clinical recommendation (80.4%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]] It adds that there is generally not enough information to report strict healthy reference ranges for species abundance (90%), discourages the Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio (86%), and finds insufficient evidence to include any dysbiosis index (90%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]
items.body: The same logic applies to any commercial panel: accuracy is measured against a reference standard in a published study, such as STARD describes; without one there is no sensitivity, specificity or LR with which to interpret the result. [[ref:bossuyt-2015-stard]] [[ref:ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2]] And even with good accuracy, if the result does not improve important outcomes there is no reason to order it. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] The same consensus discourages the test provider from giving any post-test therapeutic advice (98%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]
items.recall: What would a commercial panel have to demonstrate before its result could help you decide?
items.pearl: Before interpreting a panel, ask for two things: the accuracy study against a reference standard and the study showing it changes outcomes.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: Porcari et al. 2025, table 1: statements 6, 26, 27, 28, 30 and 32 (% Delphi agreement; no GRADE because of their conceptual content). GRADE Handbook 2013, ch. 7. STARD 2015.

items.stem: In a teaching example, a test is compared with the reference standard in 100 people: of the 10 with the disease, 7 test positive; of the 90 without it, 77 test negative. What are the sensitivity and specificity?

options.text: Sensitivity 70% and specificity 85.6%
Sensitivity 35% and specificity 96%
options.why: These are the PPV (7 of 20 positives = 35%) and the NPV (77 of 80 negatives = 96%), not sensitivity and specificity.

options.text: Sensitivity 85.6% and specificity 70%
options.why: They are swapped: sensitivity is calculated in the diseased and specificity in the non-diseased.

options.text: Sensitivity 7% and specificity 77%
options.why: These are counts out of the total of 100, not proportions within each group.

items.explanation: Sensitivity = true positives / all diseased; specificity = true negatives / all non-diseased. Predictive values use a different denominator: all positives or all negatives.

items.stem: The same test (sensitivity 70%, specificity 85.6%) is applied to 1000 people at 1% prevalence: there are 150 positives, of whom 7 have the disease. What is the PPV and what does it teach?

options.text: 4.7%: with a low pre-test probability, the vast majority of positives are false positives
options.why: Correct: 7/150 = 4.7%; 143 of the 150 positives do not have the disease.

options.text: 70%, because PPV equals sensitivity
options.why: Sensitivity is calculated among the diseased; PPV among those who test positive.

options.text: 35%, because PPV is a fixed property of the test
options.why: 35% was the PPV at 10% prevalence; PPV changes with prevalence.
That is the NPV in this scenario (847/850), not the PPV.

items.explanation: Sensitivity and specificity do not change, but PPV falls from 67.5% (30% prevalence) to 35.0% (10%) and 4.7% (1%). Testing people with a low pre-test probability fills the clinic with false positives.

items.stem: A test has 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity (numerical exercise). Your patient has a 10% pre-test probability and the result is positive. What is the post-test probability?

options.why: That would be the post-test probability if the pre-test probability were 50% (odds 1 × 9 = 9; 9/10 = 90%); equating it with sensitivity ignores the pre-test probability.
Correct: LR+ = 0.9/(1 − 0.9) = 9; pre-test odds = 0.1/0.9 = 1/9; post-test odds = 1/9 × 9 = 1; probability = 1/(1 + 1) = 50%.
Multiplying sensitivity by specificity (0.9 × 0.9) is meaningless here; you multiply the pre-test odds by the LR+.
Staying at 10% would imply an LR of 1; an LR+ of 9 does change the probability.

items.explanation: The same positive result with LR+ 9 takes you to 50% if the pre-test probability was 10% and to 90% if it was 50%. The test does not deliver “the diagnosis”: it updates the probability you already had.

items.stem: A patient brings a commercial stool panel with a high “dysbiosis index” and asks you to treat it. The laboratory publishes no study against a reference standard. What is most appropriate?

options.text: Treat, because the index is out of range
options.why: The 2025 consensus finds insufficient evidence to include dysbiosis indices or strict healthy reference ranges.

options.text: Repeat the same panel to confirm it
options.why: Repeating a test of unknown validity does not make it valid: it still has no known sensitivity, specificity or LR.

options.text: Explain that without demonstrated accuracy or an effect on outcomes the result cannot inform the decision, and return to her clinical problem
options.why: Correct: without a reference standard there is no accuracy to interpret, and GRADE adds that a test that does not improve outcomes has no reason to be used.

options.text: Order another brand's panel and compare
options.why: Two unvalidated tests do not make a reference standard.

items.explanation: The 2025 consensus does not recommend routine microbiome testing, and discourages ordering it without a clinical recommendation and providers giving therapeutic advice. The useful question is what clinical problem the patient has and what evidence exists for it.

items.title: Relative versus absolute risk
items.core: Going from a 4% to a 3% risk is a 25% relative reduction and a 1 percentage point absolute reduction: the same benefit, but the relative figure makes prescribing more tempting. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]] NAMS defines relative risk as the ratio of event rates in two groups and absolute risk as their difference, and considers absolute risk more useful for conveying risks and benefits in clinic. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.body: Relative effects tend to be more stable across risk groups than absolute ones, so the absolute benefit depends on the baseline risk: in atrial fibrillation, warfarin prevents about 70 strokes a year per 1000 high-risk patients (about 120 strokes per 1000 a year) and only 12 in low-risk patients (about 20 per 1000). [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]] NICE NG197 recommends absolute rather than relative risk: say the risk rises from 1 in 1000 to 2 in 1000, not that it doubles. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] NAMS adds that very small effects may be less clinically relevant, particularly for rare outcomes (Level I). [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.recall: A risk falls from 4% to 3%: what are the relative and the absolute reductions?
items.pearl: When you read “cuts risk by 50%”, ask: from what to what, and over what time?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Cochrane Handbook v6.5 (2024), ch. 15, sections 15.4.1 and 15.4.3. NAMS 2022, “Explaining hormone therapy risk” and key points (p. 2). NICE NG197, rec. 1.4.7 (p. 15).

items.title: Number needed to treat (NNT)
items.core: The NNT is the expected number of people who need to receive the experimental rather than the comparator intervention for one additional person to incur or avoid an event over a given time. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]] It is computed as 1 divided by the absolute value of the risk difference and always rounded up: with a difference of −0.12 the NNT is 9, and with −0.22 it is 5. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]]
items.body: If the meta-analysis gives an RR, a baseline risk has to be assumed: with RR 0.92 and an assumed comparator risk of 0.3 (300 per 1000), the effect is 24 fewer events per 1000 and the NNT is 42. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]] The NNT is comparative (against a specific comparator), it is an expected value (an NNT of 10 does not mean one event in every group of 10), and it must come with its time frame. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]] Cochrane advises against the phrase “number needed to harm” and prefers NNTB and NNTH, for an additional beneficial or harmful outcome. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]]
items.recall: How is the NNT calculated from a risk difference, and which way is it rounded?
items.pearl: An NNT without a comparator, a baseline risk and a time frame cannot be interpreted.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Cochrane Handbook v6.5 (2024), ch. 15, sections 15.4.2, 15.4.4, 15.4.4.1 and 15.4.4.2. The chapter's formulas are images that were not extracted: their text description and worked examples were used (1/0.12 = 8.3 → 9; 1/0.22 = 4.5 → 5; 1/0.024 = 41.7 → 42).

items.title: Shared decision-making step by step (NICE NG197)
items.core: NICE defines shared decision making as a collaborative process in which a person and their healthcare professional work together to reach a joint decision about care. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] When discussing tests or treatments, it recommends explaining the aims of each option, openly discussing the risks, benefits and consequences of each (including no treatment or no change), clarifying what the person hopes to gain and discussing any misconceptions. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]]
items.body:
The NG197 steps: agree an agenda and say how long the discussion will last (1.2.7); give information in manageable chunks and check understanding, for example with teach back (1.2.11); give the time needed (1.2.12); accept that the person may weigh risks and benefits differently from the professional (1.2.13); make a joint decision and agree when to review it (1.2.14); summarise at the end what has been decided and what happens next (1.2.15); and explain that they can change their mind at any time (1.2.16). [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] Decision aids should only be used if they are quality assured, reflect evidence-based best practice and are relevant to that decision and setting. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]]

GRADE notes that weak recommendations require more time for shared decision making, because not everyone is best served by the same option. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]]
items.recall: List the NICE NG197 steps for shared decision making.
items.pearl: “Doing nothing” is always an option to put on the table, with its numbers.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG197 (2021): definition (p. 5), recs 1.2.7–1.2.16 (pp. 10–12) and 1.3.1–1.3.2 (p. 13). GRADE Handbook 2013, section 6.1.2.

items.title: Communicating numbers as NICE recommends
items.core: NICE NG197 recommends using numerical data when available, because people interpret words such as “rare” or “common” differently, and doing so with absolute risk, with natural frequencies (10 in 100) rather than percentages, and with the same denominator when comparing (7 in 100 against 20 in 100, not 1 in 14 against 1 in 5). [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]]
items.body: In addition: present risk over a defined time period (if 100 people are treated for 1 year, 10 will have a given side effect), use positive and negative framing together (it works for 97 in 100 and does not work for 3 in 100), and combine numbers with pictograms. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] Information should be personalised as far as possible, making clear how it applies to the person and how much uncertainty it carries. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] Cochrane agrees that natural frequencies are the way of expressing absolute differences that healthcare consumers understand best. [[ref:cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15]]
items.recall: According to NICE, how should you present a risk to a patient?
items.pearl: Say “out of 100 women in your situation…”, not “30% more”.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG197, recs 1.4.2 and 1.4.5–1.4.11 (pp. 14–15). Cochrane Handbook v6.5 (2024), ch. 15, section 15.4.3.

items.stem: A meta-analysis gives an RR of 0.92 for an event; in your patients the baseline risk is 30% (300 per 1000). What are the absolute effect and the NNT?

options.text: 24 fewer per 1000; NNT 42
8 fewer per 100; NNT 13
options.why: It confuses the relative reduction (8%) with the absolute one; the absolute reduction is 8% of a 30% risk, that is, 2.4 points.

options.text: 24 fewer per 1000; NNT 41
options.why: By convention the NNT is always rounded up: 41.7 becomes 42.

options.text: An NNT cannot be calculated from an RR
options.why: It can, if a baseline risk is assumed; Cochrane advises doing so for a range of baseline risks.

items.explanation: From RR to NNT: risk with the intervention = baseline risk × RR; difference = baseline risk − risk with the intervention; NNT = 1 / difference, rounded up. With a different baseline risk, the same RR gives a different NNT.

items.stem: A treatment raises a side effect from 1 to 2 in every 1000 people. According to NICE NG197, how do you communicate it?

options.text: “This treatment doubles the risk”
options.why: That is relative risk; NICE recommends absolute rather than relative risk.

options.text: “The risk goes from 1 in 1000 to 2 in 1000 people”
options.why: Correct: absolute risk, in natural frequencies and with the same denominator; it is the example in recommendation 1.4.7.

options.text: “The risk increases by 100%”
options.why: It is still relative risk, and in a percentage rather than natural frequencies.

options.text: “It is a rare risk, don't worry”
options.why: NICE warns that words such as “rare” are interpreted differently and asks for numbers when available.

items.explanation: NG197: absolute risk, natural frequencies, the same denominator, a defined time period, and positive and negative framing. Here: 999 in 1000 without the side effect untreated, against 998 in 1000 treated.

items.stem: A study announces that an intervention “cuts risk by 25%”: the risk went from 4% to 3%. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The absolute reduction is 25%
options.why: 25% is the relative reduction (1 of 4); the absolute reduction is the difference, 1 point.

options.text: The relative reduction is 25% and the absolute reduction 1 percentage point (NNT 100)
options.why: Correct: (4 − 3)/4 = 25% relative; 4 − 3 = 1 point absolute; 1/0.01 = 100.

options.text: The absolute reduction is 3%
options.why: 3% is the final risk, not the difference between groups.

options.text: Relative and absolute coincide if the study is large
options.why: Study size does not change the relationship between the two measures: the absolute one depends on the baseline risk.

items.explanation: It is the Cochrane example: the same benefit sounds larger in relative terms (“25%”) than in absolute terms (“1 point”). To decide and to explain, use the absolute figure and its NNT.

items.title: Case: Julia and an antioxidant “for fragmentation”

steps.text: Julia (fictional case), 35, is about to start IVF with her partner, Adrián, who has raised sperm DNA fragmentation. She brings a website claiming that an antioxidant blend “cuts fragmentation by 40%” (fictional claim). The first thing you check is the outcome: fragmentation is a surrogate, and GRADE asks you to look for the important outcome, here live birth; ESHRE notes that many antioxidant studies used exactly these surrogates. [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

You look for the best evidence on live births: the 2022 Cochrane review finds an OR of 1.43 with very low certainty, which no longer shows an increase once the studies at high risk of bias are removed, and the ESHRE add-ons guideline concludes that antioxidants are not recommended in assisted reproduction. [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

The same website offers an “oxidative stress panel” to adjust the dose. You find no study comparing it with a reference standard or showing that it changes outcomes, so its accuracy is unknown and its result cannot guide the decision. [[ref:bossuyt-2015-stard]] [[ref:grade-2013-handbook]]

You discuss it with Julia and Adrián following NICE NG197: the options, including taking nothing, in natural frequencies and with their uncertainty. According to the Cochrane review, if 16 in 100 couples have a live birth without antioxidants, with antioxidants it would be between 17 and 27, with very low certainty and no demonstrated increase when only studies at lower risk of bias are kept; and mild gastrointestinal discomfort would go from 2 in 100 to between 2 and 7 (low certainty). They decide not to take it and agree to review the decision if better evidence appears. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]]

items.stem: A review rates the certainty of evidence for an outcome as “very low”. According to GRADE, what does this mean?

options.text: That the effect is very small, even though the estimate is precise, and therefore has no clinical relevance for any patient
options.why: Certainty measures confidence in the estimate, not the size of the effect.

options.text: That the true effect is likely to be substantially different from the estimate
options.why: Correct: this is the GRADE definition of very low.

options.text: That the study included very few patients, since GRADE assigns certainty only according to each study’s sample size
options.why: Sample size affects imprecision, but certainty is judged with five factors for rating down and three for rating up.

options.text: That the intervention is harmful and contraindicated, because very low certainty equals a recommendation against
options.why: Certainty is not a recommendation; strength is judged separately.

items.explanation: GRADE rates the certainty of evidence for each outcome at four levels: high, moderate, low and very low. High means great confidence that the true effect lies close to the estimate; very low means the true effect is likely to be substantially different.

items.stem: The same randomised trials provide data on mortality and on quality of life. Can the GRADE certainty differ between the two outcomes?

options.text: No: certainty is assigned study by study, so all outcomes from the same trial always share the same level
options.why: GRADE rates per outcome and across the body of studies, not study by study.

options.text: No: if the trials are randomised, all outcomes start and stay at high certainty with no possibility of rating down
options.why: Trials start at high certainty, but each outcome can be rated down by the five factors.

options.text: Yes, but only if the outcomes come from different trials; within the same trial certainty is necessarily identical
options.why: GRADE gives precisely the opposite example: within the same trials, outcomes can have different certainty.

options.text: Yes: it is rated per outcome, and mortality may stay at high certainty while quality of life ends up lower
options.why: Correct: this is the GRADE handbook’s example.

items.explanation: GRADE rates certainty per outcome and across the body of studies, not study by study: within the same trials, mortality may stay at high certainty while quality of life ends up lower.

items.stem: A talk presents “expert opinion” as the lowest level of the evidence pyramid. What does the GRADE handbook say?

options.text: That expert opinion is not a level of evidence but an interpretation of evidence, and the type of studies behind it should be stated
options.why: Correct: this is what the handbook states.

options.text: That expert opinion equals moderate certainty when it comes from an international panel of more than ten recognised specialists
options.why: GRADE does not turn expert opinion into a certainty level, whatever the size of the panel.

options.text: That expert opinion starts at low certainty, like observational studies, and can be rated up if there is a dose-response gradient
options.why: Observational studies start at low certainty; expert opinion is not a study design.

options.text: That expert opinion occupies the very low level, below case series, and so can never support a recommendation
options.why: The handbook does not place it as a level; it is an interpretation of evidence.

items.explanation: According to the GRADE handbook, expert opinion is not a level of evidence: it is an interpretation of evidence, and the type of studies behind it should be stated. Trials without important limitations start at high certainty, observational studies at low, and case series usually drop to very low.

items.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the five factors for which GRADE rates certainty down?

options.text: Imprecision of the estimate, for example when the confidence interval is wide and includes effects that would lead to different decisions
options.why: Imprecision is one of the five factors for rating down.

options.text: Indirectness, for example when the population, intervention or outcome studied differs from those of the clinical question
options.why: Indirectness is one of the five factors for rating down.

options.text: A large magnitude of effect
options.why: Correct: it is one of the three factors for rating certainty up.

options.text: Inconsistency between studies, that is, when the results of different studies vary importantly without explanation
options.why: Inconsistency is one of the five factors for rating down.

items.explanation: Five factors can lower certainty by one or two levels: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. Three can raise it: a large magnitude of effect, a dose-response gradient, and all plausible confounding having reduced the observed effect.

items.stem: Several observational studies with no obvious bias show a very large effect and a dose-response gradient. What does GRADE allow?

options.text: Nothing: observational studies always remain at low certainty, because only randomised trials can reach moderate or high certainty
options.why: The rating-up factors apply mainly to non-randomised studies, which can reach moderate or even high certainty.

options.text: Rate certainty up, which with large effects and no obvious bias can reach moderate or even high
options.why: Correct: a large effect and dose-response are rating-up factors.

options.text: Treat them as randomised trials from the outset, because a large effect proves by itself that there is no confounding
options.why: They do not start as trials; they are rated up from their starting level through explicit judgement.

options.text: Rate them down to very low certainty, because a very large effect in observational studies almost always indicates publication bias
options.why: A large effect without obvious bias is a reason to rate up, not down.

items.explanation: The rating-up factors (large effect, dose-response and confounding that would reduce the effect) apply mainly to non-randomised studies: with large effects and no obvious bias, they can reach moderate or even high certainty (Cochrane, ch. 14).

items.stem: A body of evidence has minor concerns about risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision, none serious on its own. What does the GRADE handbook indicate?

options.text: Rate down three levels automatically, one per factor with concerns, with no need for judgement, because GRADE would apply a fixed rule per factor
options.why: GRADE is not a quantitative system: each factor is a continuum and requires explicit judgement, although the factors are cumulative.

options.text: Rate down no levels, because only serious problems count and minor concerns are completely ignored in the rating
options.why: Minor concerns about several factors can justify rating down one level.

options.text: Exclude the studies with concerns from the analysis and rate only the remaining ones, with no need to explain the decision
options.why: The handbook does not propose excluding studies; it asks for the judgement to be explicit and transparent.

options.text: Rate down one level for one or two of those factors and explain it in a footnote, because each factor is a continuum that requires judgement
options.why: Correct: GRADE’s merit is that the judgement is explicit.

items.explanation: GRADE is not a quantitative system: each factor is a continuum that requires judgement, and its merit is that the judgement is explicit and transparent. With minor concerns about several factors, authors may rate down one level for one or two of them and explain it in a footnote.

items.stem: A guideline issues a weak (conditional) recommendation in favour of a treatment. How should you interpret it in clinic?

options.text: Most people would want the option but many would not, and each patient needs help to decide in line with her values
options.why: Correct: that is why weak recommendations require more time for shared decision making.

options.text: That the treatment does not work and the guideline mentions it only out of courtesy, so it should not be offered to any patient
options.why: A weak recommendation in favour does not mean inefficacy; it means the choice depends on values.

options.text: That the evidence is necessarily of low or very low certainty, because with high certainty all recommendations are strong
options.why: There can be weak recommendations with high-certainty evidence.

options.text: That it must be applied to every patient without exception, like a strong one, but with a somewhat lower evidence level
options.why: That does not describe a weak recommendation, and even a strong one should not be applied by rote.

items.explanation: Weak recommendations, also called conditional, mean that most people would want the option but many would not, and each patient needs help to decide in line with her values; a strong recommendation means most people should receive it. Strength depends on certainty, the balance of benefits and harms, values and preferences, and resource use.

items.stem: According to the GRADE handbook, when is a strong recommendation with low or very low certainty acceptable?

options.text: Whenever the panel agrees unanimously, because unanimity makes up for the lack of evidence
options.why: GRADE discourages it except in specific paradigmatic situations, not because of unanimity.

options.text: Never: GRADE forbids combining strong strength with low certainty, and any guideline that does so breaks the system
options.why: GRADE discourages it but exceptionally admits it in five paradigmatic situations.

options.text: Exceptionally, in five paradigmatic situations, for example a possible benefit in a life-threatening situation or possible catastrophic harm
options.why: Correct: GRADE discourages it outside those situations.

options.text: When the treatment is cheap and widely available, because low cost turns any recommendation into a strong one
options.why: Resource use influences strength, but does not by itself make a recommendation strong.

items.explanation: GRADE judges strength separately from certainty: there can be weak recommendations with high certainty and, exceptionally, strong ones with low or very low certainty, which it discourages except in five paradigmatic situations (for example, possible benefit in a life-threatening situation or possible catastrophic harm).

items.stem: In the 2023 ESHRE unexplained infertility guideline, when is evidence automatically graded as “very low (+OOO)”?

options.text: When trials include fewer than 100 patients per arm, because the guideline considers estimates imprecise below that size
options.why: The guideline uses no such threshold; the automatic grading depends on the absence of specific studies.

options.text: When there are no studies specific to unexplained infertility
options.why: Correct: that is why each recommendation’s justification is worth reading.

options.text: When the recommendation is conditional, because ESHRE assigns very low certainty to all its conditional recommendations
options.why: Strength and certainty are judged separately; there are strong recommendations with ⊕.

options.text: When the panel issues a good practice point, which in ESHRE equals very low evidence from trials
options.why: A GPP rests mainly on expert opinion, not on very-low-certainty trials.

items.explanation: ESHRE uses the same reading of “strong” and “conditional” as GRADE and automatically grades evidence as very low (+OOO) when there are no studies specific to unexplained infertility; so, faced with a “strong with ⊕” recommendation, read the justification.

items.stem: A NAMS 2022 recommendation carries Level III and an ESHRE one carries the label GPP. What do they have in common?

options.text: Both indicate good and consistent scientific evidence from large randomised trials
options.why: That is NAMS Level I; Level III and GPP rest mainly on consensus or expert opinion.

options.text: Both indicate limited or inconsistent evidence, equivalent to NAMS Level II and to GRADE moderate certainty
options.why: NAMS Level II is limited or inconsistent evidence; Level III is consensus and expert opinion.

options.text: Both are strong recommendations with high certainty, because the two scales use the same legend as GRADE
options.why: Each organisation uses its own legend; GRADE warns that letters and numbers vary widely.

options.text: Both rest mainly on consensus and expert opinion
options.why: Correct: useful, but not equivalent to trial evidence.

items.explanation: In ESHRE, GPP (good practice point) marks a recommendation based mainly on expert opinion. NAMS 2022 grades: I, good and consistent scientific evidence; II, limited or inconsistent; III, mainly consensus and expert opinion. GRADE warns that the use of letters and numbers varies widely between organisations.

items.stem: The 2023 ESHRE add-ons guideline has 42 recommendations: none on high-quality evidence and only 4 on moderate quality. What percentage relies on lower-quality evidence, experience or consensus?

options.text: 38 of 42 = 90.5% (about 90%), although the guideline’s abstract says 95%
4 of 42 = 9.5%, because the percentage is calculated from the moderate-quality recommendations, which are the ones that provide evidence
options.why: 9.5% is the moderate-quality share; the question asks for the rest.

options.text: 38 of 42 = 95%, the exact figure from the abstract, which matches the count in the recommendations table
options.why: 38 ÷ 42 is 90.5%, not 95%; the abstract gives a figure that does not match the count.

options.text: 42 of 42 = 100%, because moderate-quality evidence is also considered insufficient and is added to the rest
options.why: The 4 moderate-quality ones are not counted among the lower-quality ones.

items.explanation: 42 − 4 = 38 recommendations rely on low-quality trials, observational data, professional experience or consensus: 38 ÷ 42 = 0.905, that is, about 90% (check: 0.905 × 42 ≈ 38). The guideline’s abstract gives 95%, a figure that does not match the count.

items.stem: In the 2023 ESHRE add-ons guideline, what distinguishes “not recommended” from “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”?

options.text: Nothing: they are two ways of wording the same category, and the guideline uses them interchangeably by chapter
options.why: They are two of the four fixed phrases, with different meanings.

options.text: “Not recommended” means it can be applied after a thorough discussion of benefits and risks, with close monitoring
options.why: That describes “can be considered”.

options.text: “Not recommended” is used for safety, lack of efficacy or lack of biological rationale (research only); the other phrase may change with more evidence
options.why: Correct: these are the definitions in the guideline’s table 1.

options.text: “Currently not recommended” is the most restrictive category and forbids use even in research, unlike “not recommended”
options.why: It is the reverse: “not recommended” limits use to research settings.

items.explanation: The 2023 ESHRE add-ons guideline uses four fixed phrases: “recommended” (applicable to most patients), “can be considered” (after a thorough discussion of benefits and risks and with close monitoring), “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” (may change with more evidence) and “not recommended” (for safety, lack of efficacy or lack of biological rationale; research settings only).

items.stem: In the 2022 Cochrane review of antioxidants in subfertile men, the primary outcome was live birth, but only 12 of the 67 studies in the meta-analysis reported it. What proportion is this, and what does it imply?

options.text: 82.1%, so almost all studies measured the important outcome and semen parameters were secondary
options.why: 82.1% is the share that did not report it (55 of 67), not the share that did.

options.text: 12%, because the percentage matches the number of studies when the total is close to 100
options.why: The denominator is 67, not 100: 12 ÷ 67 = 17.9%.

options.text: 5.6%, obtained by dividing 67 by 12 and expressing it as a percentage of all trials
options.why: 67 ÷ 12 = 5.58 is a ratio, not a proportion; the proportion is 12 ÷ 67.

options.text: 17.9% (12 ÷ 67): most studies did not report live birth (only 20 reported clinical pregnancy) and focused on semen parameters, which are surrogate outcomes

items.explanation: 12 ÷ 67 = 0.179 (17.9%); 55 of 67 (82.1%) did not report live births (check: 17.9% + 82.1% = 100%). With those 12 trials, antioxidants may increase live births (OR 1.43; very low certainty), but without the studies at high risk of bias there was no longer evidence of an increase. ESHRE notes that many antioxidant studies used semen parameters or DNA fragmentation as surrogate outcomes.

items.stem: A trial of a supplement measures only sperm DNA fragmentation, with no pregnancy or live birth data. According to GRADE, how does this affect certainty?

options.text: It does not affect it, because DNA fragmentation is a validated biomarker that GRADE treats as equivalent to live birth
options.why: GRADE asks for surrogates to be used only when data on important outcomes are lacking, and they usually lower certainty.

options.text: It usually lowers it by one or two levels for indirectness, two if the surrogate is far removed in the causal pathway
options.why: Correct: this is what the GRADE handbook indicates.

options.text: It raises it by one level, because laboratory outcomes are measured more precisely than clinical ones and reduce imprecision
options.why: Using a surrogate is penalised for indirectness; it is not a rating-up factor.

options.text: It lowers it by three levels for risk of bias, because any study using a surrogate outcome is considered biased
options.why: The reason is indirectness, and the downgrade is one or two levels.

items.explanation: GRADE says surrogate outcomes should be used only when data on important outcomes are lacking and that they usually lower certainty by one or two levels for indirectness (two when the surrogate is far removed in the causal pathway). ESHRE notes that many antioxidant studies used semen parameters or the fragmentation index as success parameters rather than pregnancy rate.

items.stem: Numerical exercise: a test is compared with the reference standard in 200 women. Of the 50 with the disease, 40 test positive; of the 150 without it, 135 test negative. What are the sensitivity and specificity?

options.text: Sensitivity 90% and specificity 80%, because sensitivity uses the healthy women who test negative and specificity the diseased women
options.why: It reverses the concepts: sensitivity = 40/50 and specificity = 135/150.

options.text: Sensitivity 72.7% and specificity 93.1%, obtained by dividing true positives and negatives by all results of each sign
options.why: These are the PPV (40/55) and NPV (135/145), not sensitivity and specificity.

options.text: Sensitivity 80% (40/50) and specificity 90% (135/150)
Sensitivity 20% and specificity 67.5%, because each group is divided by the total of 200 women studied
options.why: 40/200 and 135/200 use the wrong denominator; sensitivity uses the diseased and specificity the healthy.

items.explanation: Sensitivity = true positives ÷ diseased = 40 ÷ 50 = 80%. Specificity = true negatives ÷ healthy = 135 ÷ 150 = 90%. There are 15 false positives and 10 false negatives; PPV would be 40 ÷ 55 = 72.7% and NPV 135 ÷ 145 = 93.1%.

items.stem: A highly sensitive test is negative in a patient. What follows from the SnNOut rule?

options.text: That the negative result almost rules out the disease, because a highly sensitive test is rarely negative in someone who has it
options.why: Correct: SnNOut = sensitive, negative, rules out.

options.text: That the negative result confirms the disease, because highly sensitive tests detect even the cases that have no symptoms
options.why: A negative does not confirm disease; with high sensitivity, it rules it out.

options.text: That the test must be repeated, because only specificity allows a negative result to be interpreted in any circumstance
options.why: It is high specificity that gives value to a positive (SpPIn); sensitivity gives value to the negative.

options.text: That the result adds nothing, because sensitivity is only useful for interpreting positive results
options.why: The reverse: high sensitivity gives value to a negative result.

items.explanation: A highly sensitive test is hardly ever negative in someone with the disease, so a negative result almost rules it out (SnNOut); a highly specific test is hardly ever positive in someone without it, so a positive result almost rules it in (SpPIn). Sensitivity and specificity have a limitation: they start from knowing who is ill, whereas in clinic one starts from the test result.

items.stem: Numerical exercise: a test with 80% sensitivity and 90% specificity is applied to 1000 women at 5% prevalence. What is the PPV?

options.text: 80%, because the positive predictive value always equals the test’s sensitivity, whatever the prevalence
options.why: PPV is not sensitivity and depends on prevalence.

options.text: 29.6%: 40 true positives out of 135 positives (40 + 95 false positives)
98.8%, because at low prevalence almost all positive results belong to women who are truly ill
options.why: 98.8% is the NPV (855 ÷ 865); at low prevalence, most positives are false.

options.text: 4%, obtained by multiplying the 5% prevalence by the 80% sensitivity and expressing it as a percentage
options.why: 5% × 80% = 4% is the share of true positives in the whole population (40/1000), not the PPV.

items.explanation: Diseased: 5% of 1000 = 50; true positives 0.80 × 50 = 40; false negatives 10. Healthy: 950; true negatives 0.90 × 950 = 855; false positives 95. PPV = 40 ÷ (40 + 95) = 40 ÷ 135 = 29.6%; NPV = 855 ÷ 865 = 98.8%. With a low pre-test probability, even a good test gives a low PPV.

items.stem: In the D-dimer teaching example (sensitivity 70% and specificity 85.6%, that is, 7/10 and 77/90), what happens to the NPV when prevalence rises from 1% to 30%?

options.text: It stays constant at 85.6%, because NPV equals specificity and does not depend on the population tested
options.why: NPV is not specificity and changes with prevalence.

options.text: It rises from 86.9% to 99.6%, because the more people are ill, the more reliable a negative result becomes
options.why: It reverses the direction: with higher prevalence, NPV falls.

options.text: It goes from 4.7% to 67.5%, like the PPV, because both predictive values rise together with prevalence
options.why: These are the PPV figures; NPV moves in the opposite direction.

options.text: It falls from 99.6% to 86.9%, while the PPV rises from 4.7% to 67.5%
options.why: Correct: predictive values depend heavily on prevalence.

items.explanation: With the same test, PPV is 4.7% at 1% prevalence, 35.0% at 10% and 67.5% at 30%; NPV is 99.6%, 96.2% and 86.9%. Unlike sensitivity and specificity, predictive values depend heavily on the prevalence in the tested population.

items.stem: Numerical exercise: a test has 80% sensitivity and 90% specificity. What are its likelihood ratios (LR+ and LR−)?

options.why: Correct: LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity.

options.text: LR+ = 0.90 ÷ 0.20 = 4.5; LR− = 0.10 ÷ 0.80 ≈ 0.13, because the LR+ numerator is specificity
options.why: It swaps sensitivity and specificity in the formulas.

options.text: LR+ = 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72; LR− = 0.20 × 0.10 = 0.02, because the ratios are obtained by multiplying both test properties
options.why: Likelihood ratios are divisions, not products.

options.text: They cannot be calculated without the prevalence, because likelihood ratios change with each population tested
options.why: LRs do not change with prevalence; they are calculated from sensitivity and specificity alone.

items.explanation: LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity) = 0.80 ÷ 0.10 = 8. LR− = (1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity = 0.20 ÷ 0.90 = 0.222. LRs do not change with prevalence (in the D-dimer example, with 7/10 and 77/90: LR+ 4.85 and LR− 0.35 at any prevalence).

items.stem: Numerical exercise: with the same test (LR+ = 8), your patient has a 20% pre-test probability and the result is positive. What is the post-test probability?

options.text: 160%, rounded to 100%, because the post-test probability is the pre-test probability multiplied by the LR+
options.why: The LR multiplies odds, not probabilities; a probability cannot exceed 100%.

options.text: 2%, because the post-test odds (2) are expressed directly as a percentage without converting them to probability
options.why: Odds of 2 equal a probability of 2 ÷ 3, not 2%.

options.text: 66.7%: pre-test odds 0.20 ÷ 0.80 = 0.25; × 8 = 2; probability 2 ÷ 3
options.why: Correct: odds ÷ (1 + odds) = 2 ÷ 3 = 0.667.

options.text: 28%, obtained by adding the LR+ of 8 to the 20% pre-test probability to reflect the information the test adds
options.why: LRs are not added to the probability; they multiply the odds.

items.explanation: Pre-test odds = 0.20 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = 0.25. Post-test odds = 0.25 × 8 = 2. Post-test probability = 2 ÷ (1 + 2) = 0.667 (66.7%). Check: 0.667 ÷ 0.333 = 2.

items.stem: A commercial marker advertises an LR+ of 1.1. How should this be interpreted according to Ranganathan and Aggarwal 2018?

options.text: As a very useful test to confirm the diagnosis, because any LR above 1 means a positive establishes the disease
options.why: LRs very useful for establishing a diagnosis are > 10; 1.1 barely discriminates.

options.text: As a test that barely changes probability: an LR of 1.0 adds nothing, and the further it moves from 1, the more it discriminates
options.why: Correct: LRs > 10 or < 0.1 are the very useful ones.

options.text: As a test that rules out the disease when positive, because LRs close to 1 behave the opposite way to what is expected
options.why: An LR+ of 1.1 increases probability minimally; it does not reverse it.

options.text: It cannot be interpreted without the exact prevalence, because the meaning of an LR changes with each tested population’s prevalence
options.why: LRs do not change with prevalence; what must be individualised is the pre-test probability.

items.explanation: An LR of 1.0 adds nothing; the further it moves from 1, the more it discriminates, and LRs > 10 or < 0.1 are very useful to establish or exclude a diagnosis. Moreover, an LR is only as reliable as the studies it comes from, the pre-test probability must be individualised, and there is no consensus on how to combine the LRs of several tests.

items.stem: A test with good diagnostic accuracy would not change your patient’s management with any of its possible results. What does GRADE say?

options.text: That it should be ordered anyway, because high accuracy alone justifies any test regardless of subsequent management
options.why: GRADE says the opposite: without improvement in important outcomes, there is no reason to use it.

options.text: That it should be ordered only if the patient asks, because a test’s accuracy makes it purely a matter of preference
options.why: GRADE centres the decision on whether the test improves patient-important outcomes.

options.text: That it should be assessed with a larger accuracy study before deciding, because accuracy alone determines usefulness
options.why: The best design is a trial that randomises diagnostic strategies and measures important outcomes.

options.text: That if a test does not improve patient-important outcomes there is no reason to use it, whatever its accuracy
options.why: Correct: accuracy acts as a surrogate outcome.

items.explanation: For GRADE, if a test fails to improve patient-important outcomes there is no reason to use it, whatever its accuracy; the best design to evaluate it is a trial that randomises diagnostic strategies and measures mortality, morbidity, symptoms, quality of life and resource use. When only accuracy studies exist, accuracy acts as a surrogate outcome.

items.stem: An accuracy study compares patients with confirmed disease against healthy volunteers and finds 99% specificity. What does STARD 2015 warn?

options.text: That including only healthy controls may make the estimates fail to reflect the test’s performance in clinical practice
options.why: Correct: STARD asks for how participants were identified and selected to be described.

options.text: That the healthy-control design is the reference one, because it eliminates false positives due to other diseases
options.why: By removing the patients who are confused with it in practice, it overestimates accuracy.

options.text: That 99% specificity guarantees a high PPV in any clinic, because PPV depends only on specificity
options.why: PPV depends heavily on prevalence, and the estimate may be biased.

options.text: That reporting specificity alone is enough, without confidence intervals or cut-offs, because the result is already almost perfect
options.why: STARD asks for the cut-offs and the estimates with their precision (for example, 95% CIs).

items.explanation: STARD 2015 warns that accuracy studies are also at risk of bias: if not all tested patients are analysed, or if only healthy controls are included, the estimates may not reflect performance in practice. Among its 30 items it asks for the intended use and clinical role of the test, how participants were identified, the cut-offs and whether they were pre-specified, and the estimates with their precision.

items.stem: A company offers a “functional” hormone panel with its own ranges and no published studies. Which two things should you ask for before using its result to decide?

options.text: Other patients’ reviews and the number of clinics using it, because a test’s spread demonstrates its clinical validity
options.why: Spread does not replace an accuracy study or evidence on outcomes.

options.text: The laboratory’s accreditation and the price, because an accredited laboratory guarantees that the test improves the patient’s outcomes
options.why: Analytical accreditation does not show diagnostic accuracy against a reference standard or clinical benefit.

options.text: An accuracy study against a reference standard and a study showing it changes outcomes
options.why: Correct: without a reference standard there is no sensitivity, specificity or LR, and without an effect on outcomes there is no reason to order it.

options.text: Repeat the panel twice to check it gives the same result, because reproducibility equals diagnostic validity
options.why: A reproducible result can be reproducibly wrong; validity requires a reference standard.

items.explanation: Accuracy is measured against a reference standard in a published study, as STARD describes; without one there is no sensitivity, specificity or LR with which to interpret the result. And even with good accuracy, if the result does not improve important outcomes there is no reason to order it (GRADE).

items.stem: A gut microbiome report flags several species as “outside the healthy range” and an “abnormal” Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio. What does the 2025 international consensus say?

options.text: That healthy abundance ranges are well established for most species and that the ratio is a validated marker
options.why: The consensus says there is generally not enough information for strict ranges and discourages the ratio.

options.text: That there is generally not enough information to report strict abundance ranges (90%) and that it discourages the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio (86%)
options.why: Correct: these are two consensus statements.

options.text: That the ratio is useful only if repeated monthly, because its daily variability prevents interpretation from a single sample
options.why: The consensus discourages the ratio; it does not propose repeating it.

options.text: That these findings should be treated with the supplements the report itself proposes, because the provider knows the result best
options.why: The consensus discourages the provider from including therapeutic advice (98%).

items.explanation: The 2025 consensus considers the evidence insufficient to widely recommend routine use (90%), states that there is generally not enough information to report strict abundance ranges (90%), discourages the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio (86%), finds insufficient evidence to include any dysbiosis index (90%) and discourages the provider from giving therapeutic advice (98%). These are Delphi statements, not GRADE recommendations.

items.stem: Numerical exercise: a treatment lowers a risk from 10% to 6% over one year. What are the relative reduction, the absolute reduction and the NNT?

options.text: Relative reduction 40%, absolute 4 percentage points, NNT 25 over one year
Relative reduction 4%, absolute 40% and NNT 2.5, because the difference between the two risks is the relative reduction
options.why: It swaps relative and absolute; the difference (4 points) is the absolute reduction.

options.text: Relative reduction 60%, absolute 6 points and NNT 17, because they are calculated from the risk remaining in the treated group
options.why: They are calculated from the difference (10% − 6% = 4 points), not the residual risk.

options.text: Relative reduction 40%, absolute 4 points and NNT 10, because the NNT is the inverse of the control group’s baseline risk
options.why: The NNT is the inverse of the risk difference: 1 ÷ 0.04 = 25.

items.explanation: Absolute reduction = 10% − 6% = 4 percentage points (0.04). Relative reduction = 0.04 ÷ 0.10 = 40%. NNT = 1 ÷ 0.04 = 25 (exact, no rounding) over one year. Check: 25 × 0.04 = 1 event avoided. The relative figure makes prescribing more tempting than the absolute one.

items.stem: In atrial fibrillation, warfarin has a similar relative effect in high- and low-risk patients. What does the Cochrane handbook example illustrate?

options.text: That the absolute benefit is the same in both groups, because a constant relative effect always produces the same absolute reduction
options.why: With the same relative effect, the absolute benefit depends on the baseline risk.

options.text: That more strokes are prevented in low-risk patients, because they have more room for improvement than high-risk ones
options.why: It is the reverse: about 70 per 1000 in high-risk versus 12 in low-risk patients.

options.text: That it prevents about 70 strokes a year per 1000 high-risk patients and only 12 in low-risk ones: absolute benefit depends on baseline risk
options.why: Correct: relative effects are more stable than absolute ones.

options.text: That the relative effect loses validity in low-risk patients, so warfarin does not reduce their risk
options.why: The relative effect holds; what changes is the absolute number of events prevented.

items.explanation: Relative effects tend to be more stable across risk groups than absolute ones, so the absolute benefit depends on the baseline risk: warfarin prevents about 70 strokes a year per 1000 high-risk patients (about 120 strokes per 1000 a year) and only 12 in low-risk patients (about 20 per 1000).

items.stem: What does NAMS 2022 say about conveying the risks and benefits of hormone therapy?

options.text: That relative risk is more useful in clinic, because patients understand percentage changes better than absolute figures
options.why: NAMS considers absolute risk more useful.

options.text: That it defines absolute risk as the ratio of event rates and relative risk as their difference, and prefers the relative one in clinic
options.why: It reverses the definitions: relative is the ratio and absolute the difference.

options.text: That any statistically significant effect is clinically relevant, also for rare outcomes, regardless of its size
options.why: NAMS notes that very small effects may be less clinically relevant, particularly for rare outcomes (Level I).

options.text: That absolute risk is more useful to convey them, and that very small effects may be less relevant for rare outcomes (Level I)
options.why: Correct: this is the NAMS position.

items.explanation: NAMS 2022 defines relative risk as the ratio of event rates in two groups and absolute risk as their difference, and considers absolute risk more useful for conveying risks and benefits in clinic; it adds that very small effects may be less clinically relevant, particularly for rare outcomes (Level I).

items.stem: Numerical exercise: a trial gives a risk difference of −0.07 (7 percentage points fewer events with treatment). What is the NNT according to the Cochrane handbook?

options.text: 14, because 1 ÷ 0.07 = 14.3 and the NNT is rounded to the nearest whole number like any other result
options.why: The handbook states that, by convention, the NNT is rounded up, not to the nearest integer.

options.text: 15: 1 ÷ 0.07 = 14.3, rounded up by convention
options.why: Correct: as in the handbook’s examples (8.3 → 9; 4.5 → 5).

options.text: 7, because the NNT equals the number of percentage points of difference between treated and control groups
options.why: The NNT is the inverse of the risk difference, not the difference itself.

options.text: −14.3, because the NNT keeps the negative sign of the risk difference to indicate that treatment reduces events
options.why: The absolute value of the difference is used and rounded up.

items.explanation: The NNT is 1 divided by the absolute value of the risk difference, rounded up by convention: 1 ÷ 0.07 = 14.29 → 15 (check: 15 × 0.07 = 1.05 ≥ 1; 14 × 0.07 = 0.98 < 1). In the handbook, with −0.12 the NNT is 9 and with −0.22 it is 5.

items.stem: Numerical exercise: a meta-analysis gives an RR of 0.75 and the baseline risk in your patients is 8% (80 per 1000). What are the absolute effect and the NNT?

options.text: 75 fewer per 1000 and NNT 14, because the RR expressed per 1000 directly equals the number of events prevented
options.why: The RR is not a number of events; it must be applied to the baseline risk.

options.text: 60 fewer per 1000 and NNT 17, because the absolute effect is the expected risk in the treated group
options.why: 60 per 1000 is the expected risk with treatment; the effect is the difference, 20 per 1000.

options.text: An NNT cannot be calculated from an RR, because the RR is a relative effect with no absolute equivalent
options.why: It can, by assuming a baseline risk, as the handbook shows.

options.text: 20 fewer per 1000 (80 − 60) and NNT 50

items.explanation: Risk with treatment = 0.75 × 80 per 1000 = 60 per 1000. Absolute effect = 80 − 60 = 20 fewer per 1000 (0.02). NNT = 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 (exact). Check: 50 × 0.02 = 1. This is the same procedure as in the Cochrane handbook (RR 0.92 with baseline risk 300 per 1000: 24 fewer per 1000, NNT 42).

items.stem: A leaflet claims that a treatment has an “NNT of 10”. Which interpretation is correct according to the Cochrane handbook?

options.text: It is an expected value against a specific comparator over a given time; it does not mean one event in every group of 10
options.why: Correct: without a comparator, baseline risk and time frame, it cannot be interpreted.

options.text: It means that in every group of 10 treated patients exactly one avoids the event, whatever the study’s follow-up period
options.why: The NNT is an expected value, not an exact rule for every group of 10, and it needs a time frame.

options.text: It is a fixed property of the treatment that does not depend on the comparator or the baseline risk of the population
options.why: The NNT is comparative and depends on the baseline risk.

options.text: It indicates that the treatment harms one in every 10 patients, which the handbook calls the “number needed to harm”
options.why: The handbook advises against “number needed to harm” and prefers NNTB and NNTH.

items.explanation: The NNT is the expected number of people who need to receive the experimental rather than the comparator intervention for one additional person to incur or avoid an event over a given time. It is comparative, it is an expected value (an NNT of 10 does not mean one event in every group of 10) and it must come with its time frame. The handbook advises against “number needed to harm” and prefers NNTB and NNTH.
