items.stem: At the end of a shared decision-making consultation about a treatment, what does NICE NG197 recommend?

options.text: Hand over the decision in writing as final, because changing it later would cause confusion and loss of adherence
options.why: NICE asks you to explain that the person can change their mind at any time (1.2.16).

options.text: Decide on the patient’s behalf if she weighs the risks differently, to ensure the option with most evidence
options.why: NICE asks you to accept that the person may weigh risks and benefits differently from the professional (1.2.13).

options.text: Summarise what was decided and what happens next, agree when to review it and explain that she can change her mind at any time
options.why: Correct: this corresponds to 1.2.14–1.2.16.

options.text: Hand over any decision aid available online, even if not quality assured, so the patient can learn more
options.why: NICE asks for only quality-assured, evidence-based decision aids relevant to that decision to be used.

items.explanation: The NICE NG197 steps include agreeing an agenda and its length (1.2.7), giving information in manageable chunks and checking understanding (1.2.11), giving the time needed (1.2.12), accepting that the person may weigh things differently (1.2.13), making a joint decision and agreeing when to review it (1.2.14), summarising what was decided and what happens next (1.2.15) and explaining that they can change their mind at any time (1.2.16).

items.stem: When presenting treatment options to a patient, what does NICE NG197 include, and what does GRADE add about weak recommendations?

options.text: Present only the option the guideline recommends most strongly, because showing alternatives without evidence confuses the patient
options.why: NICE asks for each option to be discussed, including no treatment or no change.

options.text: Discuss the risks, benefits and consequences of each option, including no treatment or no change; weak recommendations require more time for shared decision making
options.why: Correct: “doing nothing” is always an option, with its numbers.

options.text: Leave out uncommon risks so as not to frighten the patient, because NICE recommends focusing the conversation on benefits
options.why: NICE asks for risks, benefits and consequences to be discussed openly.

options.text: Give all the information in a single block at the start, because breaking it up lengthens the visit without improving understanding
options.why: NICE asks for information in manageable chunks with checks of understanding, for example with teach back.

items.explanation: NICE NG197 defines shared decision making as a collaborative process and recommends explaining the aims of each option, openly discussing its risks, benefits and consequences (including no treatment or no change), clarifying what the person hopes to gain and discussing misconceptions. GRADE notes that weak recommendations require more time for shared decision making, because not everyone is best served by the same option.

items.stem: You want to compare two risks expressed as “1 in 14” and “1 in 5”. How would you present them according to NICE NG197?

options.text: With the same denominator: about 7 in 100 against 20 in 100 (1 ÷ 14 ≈ 0.071; 1 ÷ 5 = 0.20)
options.why: Correct: this is the NICE example.

options.text: As they are, because fractions with different denominators are easier to compare as they are small numbers
options.why: NICE expressly asks for the same denominator to be used when comparing.

options.text: With words such as “uncommon” and “common”, because patients interpret words more uniformly than numbers
options.why: NICE notes that people interpret such words differently and prefers numbers.

options.text: As a relative risk: “the second risk is almost three times higher”, because it sums up the comparison in a single figure
options.why: NICE recommends absolute rather than relative risk.

items.explanation: NICE NG197 recommends using numerical data when available, in absolute risk, with natural frequencies and with the same denominator when comparing: 7 in 100 against 20 in 100, not 1 in 14 against 1 in 5 (1 ÷ 14 = 0.071 ≈ 7 in 100; 1 ÷ 5 = 20 in 100).

items.stem: Which of these ways of communicating an effect best follows NICE NG197?

options.text: “It works in 97% of cases”, without mentioning in how many it does not, so as not to raise unnecessary doubts
options.why: NICE asks for positive and negative framing to be used together.

options.text: “It reduces side effects by 30%”, because the relative reduction is what patients understand best according to NICE and Cochrane
options.why: NICE recommends absolute risk, and Cochrane notes that natural frequencies are what is best understood.

options.text: “If 100 people take it for 1 year, it works for 97 and does not work for 3”, accompanied by a pictogram
options.why: Correct: defined time period, dual framing, natural frequencies and a pictogram.

options.text: “It is a very effective treatment and side effects are rare”, because avoiding numbers makes the information easier to understand
options.why: NICE recommends numbers, because words such as “rare” are interpreted differently.

items.explanation: NICE NG197 asks for risk over a defined time period (if 100 people are treated for 1 year, 10 will have a side effect), positive and negative framing together (it works for 97 in 100 and does not work for 3 in 100), numbers combined with pictograms, and personalised information. Cochrane agrees that natural frequencies are the way of expressing absolute differences that is best understood.

bossuyt-2015-stard.title: STARD 2015: an updated list of essential items for reporting diagnostic accuracy studies
bossuyt-2015-stard.authors: Bossuyt PM, Reitsma JB, Bruns DE, Gatsonis CA, Glasziou PP, Irwig L, Lijmer JG, Moher D, Rennie D, de Vet HC, Kressel HY, Rifai N, Golub RM, Altman DG, Hooft L, Korevaar DA, Cohen JF; STARD Group
bossuyt-2015-stard.population: Authors, editors and readers of diagnostic accuracy studies (an index test against a reference standard).
bossuyt-2015-stard.finding: List of 30 essential items for reporting a diagnostic accuracy study, including the intended use and clinical role of the test, how participants were identified, the reference standard, positivity cut-offs, blinding, the cross tabulation of results against the reference standard, and the precision of estimates. These studies are at risk of bias: if not all tested patients are analysed, or if only healthy controls are included, the accuracy estimates may not reflect the test's real performance.
bossuyt-2015-stard.limitations: Full text read (BMJ 2015;351:h5527, Europe PMC version PMC4623764). It is a reporting guideline, not a risk-of-bias tool or a clinical guideline.

cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14.title: Chapter 14: Completing ‘Summary of findings’ tables and grading the certainty of the evidence. Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions version 6.5
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14.authors: Schünemann HJ, Higgins JP, Vist GE, Glasziou P, Akl EA, Skoetz N, Guyatt GH
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14.population: Authors and readers of Cochrane intervention reviews: summary of findings tables and certainty assessment with GRADE.
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14.finding: Cochrane adopts GRADE: four certainty levels for each outcome (high, moderate, low, very low), five domains for rating down (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias) and, for non-randomised and rarely randomised studies, three domains for rating up. Sound non-randomised studies are usually graded low; with large effects and no obvious bias they may be rated moderate or even high.
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch14.limitations: Web text of the chapter read (last updated August 2023, in version 6.5, 2024). Figures were read as text; some formulas and images were not extracted.

cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15.title: Chapter 15: Interpreting results and drawing conclusions. Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions version 6.5
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15.authors: Schünemann HJ, Vist GE, Higgins JP, Santesso N, Deeks JJ, Glasziou P, Akl EA, Guyatt GH
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15.population: Authors and readers of Cochrane reviews: interpreting confidence intervals, relative and absolute measures, number needed to treat and conclusions.
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15.finding: A risk reduction from 4% to 3% is a 25% relative reduction and a 1 percentage point absolute reduction; a risk ratio of 0.75 equals a 25% relative risk reduction. The NNT is the expected number of people who need to receive the experimental rather than the comparator intervention for one additional person to incur or avoid an event over a given time; it is computed from the absolute value of the risk difference and rounded up (risk difference −0.12: NNT 9; −0.22: NNT 5). With RR 0.92 and an assumed comparator risk of 0.3, the effect is 24 fewer per 1000 and the NNT is 42. Relative effects are more stable across risk groups than absolute ones, so absolute benefit should be expressed for each baseline risk; natural frequencies are understood best.
cochrane-2024-handbook-ch15.limitations: Web text of the chapter read (last updated August 2023, in version 6.5, 2024). The formulas are images and were not extracted: only the chapter's text description and its own numerical examples were used.

deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.title: Antioxidants for male subfertility
deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.authors: de Ligny W, Smits RM, Mackenzie-Proctor R, Jordan V, Fleischer K, de Bruin JP, Showell MG
deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.population: 90 RCTs, 10,303 subfertile men (aged 18–65) of couples attending fertility clinics, some undergoing assisted reproduction; 20 different oral antioxidants. Excluded men with idiopathic infertility and normal semen parameters. Search to 15 Feb 2021. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;5:CD007411.
deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.finding: Live birth: OR 1.43 (95% CI 1.07–1.91; 12 RCTs; 1283 men; very low certainty; 246 live births); with a 16% baseline, 17–27% with antioxidants. Excluding high risk-of-bias studies: no evidence of increase (Peto OR 1.22; 95% CI 0.85–1.75; 8 RCTs; 827 men). Clinical pregnancy: OR 1.89 (1.45–2.47; 20 RCTs; 1706 men; low certainty). Miscarriage: no difference (OR 1.46; 0.75–2.83; 6 RCTs; very low certainty). Mild gastrointestinal discomfort: OR 2.70 (1.46–4.99; 16 RCTs; low certainty). Only 20 of 67 meta-analysed studies reported clinical pregnancy and 12 live birth. Authors' conclusion: overall evidence inconclusive owing to serious risk of bias and imprecision.
deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.limitations: Full abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 35506389; text saved in the source library), including the sensitivity analysis and the authors’ conclusions; ESHRE add-ons 2023 reproduces the live-birth, miscarriage and gastrointestinal figures. Full text, GRADE tables and semen-parameter results not read. Antioxidants and doses highly heterogeneous; excluded men with idiopathic infertility and normal semen parameters.

eshre-2023-addons.title: Good practice recommendations on add-ons in reproductive medicine
eshre-2023-addons.authors: ESHRE Add-ons Working Group; Lundin K, Bentzen JG, Bozdag G, Ebner T, Harper J, Le Clef N, Moffett A, Norcross S, Polyzos NP, Rautakallio-Hokkanen S, Sfontouris I, Sermon K, Vermeulen N, Pinborg A
eshre-2023-addons.population: Patients undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART); Hum Reprod 2023 (ESHRE Pages).
eshre-2023-addons.finding: 42 recommendations using its own four-phrase scale (recommended; can be considered; currently not recommended for routine clinical use; not recommended). Peripheral blood immune tests and uterine NK-cell testing: not recommended. Screening hysteroscopy: currently not recommended for routine clinical use (can be considered in recurrent implantation failure). Sperm DNA damage testing, endometrial scratching and KIR/HLA genotyping: currently not recommended for routine clinical use. ICSI for non-male factor infertility: not recommended.
eshre-2023-addons.limitations: Full text read (UCL Discovery open-access copy of the advance online version); the wording of every cited recommendation and the scale-definition table were checked verbatim. Good practice recommendations based on review and consensus, not a GRADE guideline: no recommendation rests on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence. ART population, not specifically unexplained infertility.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

grade-2013-handbook.title: GRADE Handbook: handbook for grading the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations using the GRADE approach
grade-2013-handbook.authors: Schünemann H, Brożek J, Guyatt G, Oxman A (editors); GRADE Working Group
grade-2013-handbook.population: Methods handbook for authors of systematic reviews, guidelines and health technology assessments who use GRADE: intervention and diagnostic test questions.
grade-2013-handbook.finding: Four levels of quality (certainty) of evidence: high, moderate, low and very low (table 5.1). Randomised trials without important limitations start as high quality and observational studies as low; five factors can lower it by 1 or 2 levels (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias) and three can raise it (large effect, dose-response gradient, residual confounding that would reduce the effect). The strength of a recommendation (strong or weak/conditional) is judged separately from quality: weak recommendations with high-quality evidence and strong ones with low or very low quality are both possible. Surrogate outcomes are used only when data on important outcomes are lacking and usually lower quality by 1 or 2 levels for indirectness. If a test fails to improve patient-important outcomes there is no reason to use it, whatever its accuracy.
grade-2013-handbook.limitations: Full web text read (version updated October 2013). The site itself warns that the handbook is being replaced by the GRADE Book (available since 2024 at book.gradepro.org) and will be phased out; sections 1, 2, 3, 5 (including 5.2) and 8 are marked as rewritten there. The definitions of certainty levels and of the factors for rating down or up match chapter 14 of the Cochrane Handbook (2024); those on strength of recommendation, surrogate outcomes, expert opinion and diagnostic tests come from this handbook only. It says “quality” where newer texts say “certainty”.

nams-2022-hormone-therapy.title: The 2022 hormone therapy position statement of The North American Menopause Society
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.authors: The 2022 Hormone Therapy Position Statement Advisory Panel of The North American Menopause Society (now The Menopause Society); Faubion SS (lead), Crandall CJ, Davis L, El Khoudary SR, Hodis HN, Lobo RA, Maki PM, Manson JE, Pinkerton JV, Santoro NF, Shifren JL, Shufelt CL, Thurston RC, Wolfman W
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.population: Perimenopausal and postmenopausal women considering hormone therapy, in the United States context (FDA indications). Position statement by an expert panel of The North American Menopause Society, approved by its Board of Trustees; Menopause 2022;29(7):767-794. Updates the 2017 statement.
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.finding: Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and the genitourinary syndrome of menopause, and prevents bone loss and fracture. In women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset without contraindications, the benefit-risk ratio is favourable; when started after 60 or more than 10 years from menopause it appears less favourable because of greater absolute risks of coronary heart disease, stroke, venous thromboembolism and dementia. Women with a uterus need adequate progestogen. It does not need to be routinely stopped at 60–65. Compounded “bioidentical” hormones raise safety concerns, and saliva or urine testing to set the dose is unreliable.
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.limitations: Full PDF (28 pp.) read on the society's website. It is a consensus position statement, not a guideline with a formal systematic review: the “Key points” carry levels I (good and consistent evidence), II (limited or inconsistent) and III (consensus and expert opinion), with no separate strength grade. Much of the risk data comes from the WHI trials (oral conjugated equine estrogens and medroxyprogesterone acetate). US regulatory context. It was the current version as of 14-10-2026 (the society has published no later one).

nice-2021-ng197.title: Shared decision making. NICE guideline NG197
nice-2021-ng197.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2021-ng197.population: People using healthcare services and the professionals and organisations of the English health service (NHS); all decisions about tests, treatments and interventions.
nice-2021-ng197.finding: Shared decision making is a collaborative process in which a person and their healthcare professional work together to reach a joint decision. In practice: agree an agenda, explain the aims of each option, discuss openly the risks, benefits and consequences of each (including no treatment or no change), clarify what the person hopes to gain, give information in chunks and check understanding (teach back), give time, accept that their views may differ from the professional's, make a joint decision and agree when to review it, and make clear they can change their mind (1.2.7–1.2.16). To communicate risk: absolute rather than relative risk, natural frequencies, the same denominator, a defined time period and both positive and negative framing (1.4.5–1.4.11).
nice-2021-ng197.limitations: Full PDF read (32 pp., published 17 June 2021). It is an English health-service guideline: several recommendations are organisational (section 1.1) and are not cited here. The accompanying evidence reviews were not read.

porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.title: International consensus statement on microbiome testing in clinical practice
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.authors: Porcari S, Mullish BH, Asnicar F, Ng SC, Zhao L, Hansen R, O'Toole PW, Raes J, Hold G, Putignani L, et al.; Cammarota G, Gasbarrini A, Ianiro G
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.population: Microbiome testing (mainly gut) in clinical practice; 69 experts from 18 countries, Delphi consensus. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025;10(2):154-167.
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.finding: There is insufficient evidence to widely recommend routine microbiome testing (90%). It discourages direct patient requests without a clinical recommendation (80.4%), therapeutic advice from the provider (98%), the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio (86%), dysbiosis indices (90%) and strict healthy reference ranges (90%). Multiplex PCR and cultures are not microbiome testing (90%); vaginal samples should be processed according to existing evidence and indications (97.5%).
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.limitations: The accepted author manuscript on PMC (PMC12343204) was read, not the typeset version; appendices not included. Expert-opinion statements (Delphi, ≥ 80% threshold), not GRADE recommendations; focused on the gut microbiome rather than vaginal or endometrial microbiome.

ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1.title: Common pitfalls in statistical analysis: Understanding the properties of diagnostic tests - Part 1
ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1.population: Teaching statistics article for clinicians (Perspect Clin Res 2018;9(1):40-43); hypothetical example of D-dimer against perfusion scanning in pulmonary embolism.
ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1.finding: Sensitivity: proportion of people with the disease (by the reference standard) who test positive (7/10 = 70% in the example); specificity: proportion without the disease who test negative (77/90 = 85.6%). PPV and NPV: probability of disease with a positive test (7/20 = 35%) or of no disease with a negative test (77/80 = 96%). Sensitivity and specificity are usually not influenced by prevalence; predictive values are: at 1% prevalence the PPV falls to 7/150 = 4.7% and the NPV is 847/850 = 99.6%. A test is best applied to people with a high pre-test probability.
ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-1.limitations: Full text read (Europe PMC, PMC5799952). The tables were not extracted, but every figure used appears in the text. Hypothetical teaching example, not clinical D-dimer data.

ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2.title: Understanding the properties of diagnostic tests - Part 2: Likelihood ratios
ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2.population: Teaching statistics article for clinicians (Perspect Clin Res 2018;9(2):99-102); continues the hypothetical D-dimer example.
ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2.finding: LR+ = sensitivity/(1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity)/specificity. In the example, LR+ = (7/10)/(13/90) = 4.85 and LR− = (3/10)/(77/90) = 0.35, unchanged at prevalences of 1%, 10% and 30%. An LR of 1.0 changes nothing; LRs > 10 or < 0.1 are very useful to rule in or rule out. Post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR; odds = probability/(1 − probability); probability = odds/(1 + odds). With a positive D-dimer, the post-test probability is 67% when the pre-test probability is 30% and 5% when it is 1%. The accuracy of LRs depends on the quality of the studies they come from.
ranganathan-2018-diagnostic-tests-2.limitations: Full text read (Europe PMC, PMC5950618). The tables were not extracted; the figures used appear in the text. Hypothetical teaching example.
